prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After reading all eight first-round statements and the chair's questions, I keep B022 with Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye as a single prize part. The mandate as I read it asks for an original, experimentally verified invention or discovery. Here the original step is Katori's proposal that trapping neutral atoms in a lattice at the magic wavelength cancels the light shift between the clock states while the tight confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects, together with his first strontium demonstrations. The decisive experimental step is the demonstration, mainly by Ye's group, that the systematic shifts can be controlled to 10^-18, including the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and the many-body regime. This has been reproduced and compared at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, so verification is a matter of record rather than expectation. It is a tool that opens a door, in the sense I care about: it lets us see time dilation across a millimetre and sets limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter that were out of reach. The two-name credit follows the two decisive steps and no one else on the shortlist offers a comparably clean allocation. I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1. I have changed one alternative: B020 replaces B038, because the chair's summary shows that the unresolved MgO priority among Parkin, Yuasa and Djayaprawira still keeps B038 from being a defensible fallback, whereas B020 is the most-named reserve and I have thought about what it would take.
statement.case_against: My reservations remain the same and I do not think the exchange has removed them. First, lineage: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and the 2012 prize the control of single quantum systems including ion clocks, and a sceptic can read the lattice clock as the next increment. I judge the lattice architecture to be distinct, since those prizes enabled the clock rather than recognising the many-atom magic-wavelength route, but the citation must make that distinction explicit. Second, the discovery content so far is mostly consistency tests and upper limits, as Pearce and Eriksson say; no new effect has been observed. Third, credit is not fully verified from the packet. Lemonde and SYRTE, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom are all named by colleagues, and I cannot settle early priority between Katori's 2001 to 2003 proposal and parallel ideas without the original papers. Fourth, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the societal benefit is prospective, although the scientific benefit is demonstrated.

responses.point: Pearce concedes that the discovery content of B022 is mostly upper limits and consistency tests with no new effect observed, and that Ye's share is partly the work of a large JILA team.
responses.response: I accept the first point. What is demonstrated is a measurement capability, and the citation should say so rather than imply a discovery of new physics. What has been observed, not merely hoped for, is the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and the many-body clock regime, and I would name the achievement as an invention and its demonstrated performance. On the large JILA team, the prize rules limit us to three names and the committee has to credit the person who led the programme and published the decisive uncertainty evaluations. That is Ye. I would not add JILA team members, but I would ask that we confirm in the evaluation papers that the 10^-18 result is attributed to his group as the originating laboratory, because I am relying on the packet and my own recollection and not on the originals.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is clearly distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes because it is a different route to precision, many neutral atoms in a lattice, and he discloses a mild link to the JILA community through John Hall.
responses.response: I agree on the distinction and I think the citation should carry it in its wording: the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping is a specific architecture. That answers the chair's first question better than a generic phrase about precision timekeeping. On the disclosure, I think disclosure is sufficient. Kroll states no supervisory or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye, and a year in Hall's laboratory during a doctorate is a field connection, not a stake in this prize. I would keep it on record and ask no further step, and I would note that Hall's own recognition is the 2005 prize, which Kroll is not asking us to revisit.

responses.point: Johansson asks whether the committee should wait for the SI redefinition of the second as an external endorsement, and says B020 would be the more conceptually rich alternative if B022 is judged a tool.
responses.response: I would not wait. The test in the statutes is a verified discovery or invention, and verification here is independent clock-to-clock agreement at the 10^-18 level, which already exists. Waiting would also hand our timetable to a metrology body whose decision depends on other considerations, such as the readiness of comparison links. I do take his second point seriously, and I have moved B020 into my alternatives for that reason. But B020 has five credited names and, as the chair notes, no agreed three, so it cannot be treated as an equal-readiness choice without arbitrary exclusions.

responses.point: Danielsson wants the citation to include a forward-looking phrase, 'opening new precision tests of nature', and admits he is working from recollection on the credit split.
responses.response: I would resist the forward-looking phrase. Our citations should describe what has been done and verified, and the tests of varying constants and dark matter are so far limits. I would also prefer the citation to name magic-wavelength trapping, which is the original idea and the thing that distinguishes the clock from its predecessors. I share his caution on recollection, so I suggest that before the vote the committee confirm from the original publications the sequence of Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice clock, the JILA and RIKEN results around 2005 to 2006, and the SYRTE work. If that record showed that another group had independently reached the lattice-clock demonstration first, I would reconsider the names.

responses.point: Lindroth resists widening the credit beyond Katori and Ye, while noting that the weighting between Katori's concept and Ye's 10^-18 performance still has to be settled.
responses.response: I agree with keeping two names. The weighting question is real, and I think the citation's two clauses answer it: invention of the lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping reflects Katori's original contribution, and development to 10^-18 reflects the record-regime work led by Ye. I would not make either part of the citation subordinate to the other. This is also the point where members who want 'invention' and those who want 'development' can both accept the same sentence, which is what the chair's first question asks for.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that a precision-measurement invention, with no new phenomenon yet observed, meets the discovery-or-invention criterion; I judge it does, but this is a judgement and not a fact.

Whether the original papers show that any other group (SYRTE, or an earlier independent lattice-clock proposal or demonstration) has a priority claim that should change the two names; the packet cannot settle this.
Whether the large JILA team makes Ye's share a fair single credit for the 10^-18 result.
If B022 fails to carry, whether B020 can be reduced to three defensible names, or whether B043 is better placed, given the unresolved Stuttgart versus later quantum-sensing credit.
statement.conflict_note: I have no known collaboration, institutional or student link to Hidetoshi Katori or Jun Ye, and no recusal issue on B022. I note again that Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague and Mehlig is in the neighbouring Gothenburg environment, neither of which bears on B022. I have professional familiarity with solid-state and materials work such as B038, but no direct tie to its credited names, and none to B020 or B043. Kroll's disclosed link through John Hall to the JILA community is in my view adequately handled by disclosure.
